evidence.observation: New table-driven fixture block `describe("settings precedence", ...)` defines the `themePrecedenceCases` table with four rows covering the full resolution order for the `theme` setting: (1) built-in default (expected `undefined`), (2) a user/global value that wins over the default, (3) a project value that wins over the user value, (4) an explicit CLI value that wins over the project value. Each row carries `userTheme`, `projectTheme`, `cliTheme` and `expected`, so the same assertion is applied to every layer of the precedence chain.

`it.each(themePrecedenceCases)` turns the table into one test per row. Each run writes `agentDir/settings.json` (user/global) and/or `projectDir/.pi/settings.json` (project) as the row requires, creates the manager with `SettingsManager.create(projectDir, agentDir)`, applies the CLI layer via `manager.applyOverrides({ theme: cliTheme })` only for the row that supplies `cliTheme`, and asserts `manager.getTheme()` equals the row's `expected`. This is the assertion that a fixture's project value beats user/default but loses to an explicit CLI value.

`applyOverrides(overrides)` re-runs `deepMergeSettings(this.settings, overrides)` over the already user+project merged settings and keeps the result in memory only (no write, no markModified). It is therefore the correct stand-in for the top, explicit-CLI precedence layer: a later merge applied on top of the file-derived value wins, and the following `save()`/`reload()` would discard it.

`getTheme()` reads `this.settings.theme` (the deep-merged global+project value, plus any in-memory overrides) and returns it unless it is a slash-separated automatic theme. Because it reads exactly the merged object that `create()` (project over global) and `applyOverrides()` (CLI over project) populate, it is the observable used by the new table to prove project > user/default and CLI > project.

claims.claim: The new `describe("settings precedence")` block is table-driven: the `themePrecedenceCases` table holds one row per precedence layer, and `it.each(themePrecedenceCases)` asserts each row against `manager.getTheme()`. Rows 3 and 4 encode the requested contract directly: the project value (`project-theme`) wins over the user/global value (`user-theme`) and over the default, while an explicit CLI value (`cli-theme`, applied through `applyOverrides`) wins over the project value.

The precedence order the table pins down matches the source: project settings are deep-merged over the user/global settings when the manager is created, and an explicit CLI value is layered on top via `applyOverrides`, which deep-merges in memory without persisting. `getTheme()` observes the resulting merged `theme`. Hence CLI > project > user > default for this fixture.

The four rows are discriminating: they use four distinct expected values (undefined, "user-theme", "project-theme", "cli-theme"), so a wrong ordering (for example project failing to override user, or CLI failing to override project) would fail at least one row instead of silently passing.
